topic: The Elegance of Dandelin Spheres: Proving Conic Sections
target_audience: High school students (Advanced Geometry) and undergraduate math enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Elegance of Dandelin Spheres: Proving Conic Sections
outline.target_audience: High school students (Advanced Geometry) and undergraduate math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Slice: From 3D to 2D
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept of a 'conic section' by intersecting a double cone with a plane. Focus on the visual formation of an ellipse and define it by its locus: the set of points where the sum of distances to two foci is constant.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Geometric Chef' slicing a perfectly conical carrot at an angle with a laser; the resulting cross-section is a smooth, purple-edged ellipse.

sections.title: The Magic Spheres Appear
sections.content: Introduce the Dandelin Spheres: two spheres placed inside the cone, one above the plane and one below. Each sphere is 'inscribed' so it is tangent to the cone (along a circle) and tangent to the cutting plane at exactly one point ($F_1$ and $F_2$).
sections.example: Visualize two glowing soap bubbles inflating inside a glass cone until they are snugly trapped by a tilted glass shelf (the plane).

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Ice Cream Cone Lemma
sections.content: Establish the critical geometric tool: tangents from a single point to a sphere are equal in length. This is essential for the transition to the formal proof.
sections.example: An ant standing at a point $P$ outside a sphere measures the distance to the 'horizon' of the sphere; no matter which direction it looks, the distance to the touch-point is identical.

sections.title: The Visual Proof: Linking Segments
sections.content: Pick an arbitrary point $P$ on the ellipse. Draw segments $PF_1$ and $PF_2$. Show that $PF_1$ is equal to the segment along the cone's surface to the upper circle of contact ($PA$), and $PF_2$ is equal to the segment to the lower circle ($PB$).
sections.example: Use color-coded neon lines: $PF_1$ (blue) and $PF_2$ (red) magically 'fold' onto the surface of the cone to form a single straight line segment $AB$ along the slant height.

sections.title: The Constant Sum
sections.content: Demonstrate that the total length $PF_1 + PF_2$ is always equal to the distance $AB$ along the cone's slant height between the two contact circles. Since the circles are fixed, this distance is constant regardless of where $P$ is moved.
sections.example: A 'Space Navigator' notices that as their ship travels the elliptical orbit ($P$), the combined length of the two fuel tethers ($PF_1$ and $PF_2$) remains as rigid as a fixed metal rod.

sections.title: Universal Application: Parabolas and Hyperbolas
sections.content: Briefly extend the logic: explain that by tilting the plane further, we interact with the spheres differently to create parabolas or hyperbolas, proving all conic sections share this spherical harmony.
sections.example: The 'Geometric Chef' tilts the laser slice more steeply; the soap bubbles shift, and the ellipse 'snaps' into an open parabola, like a spotlight hitting a stage floor.

storyboard.title: The Slice: From 3D to 2D
lecture_lines: A conic section forms where a plane slices a cone.
Tilting the plane creates different geometric curves.
An ellipse is defined by a constant distance sum.
animations: Draw a white triangle (#FFFFFF) representing a cone and a green line (#00FF00) representing a cutting plane.
Animate a purple ellipse (#800080) appearing at the intersection area between the cone and plane.
Highlight two yellow points F1 and F2 (#FFFF00) on the plane to indicate future foci.

storyboard.title: The Magic Spheres Appear
lecture_lines: Place two spheres inside the cone, above and below.
Inflate them until they touch the cone's surface.
Each sphere also touches the tilted cutting plane.
They are tangent to the plane at points $F_1, F_2$.
These tangent points are the foci of our ellipse.
animations: Show the cone and plane; draw a small yellow circle (#FFFF00) tangent to both cone walls and the plane.
Draw a larger cyan circle (#0000FF) below the plane, tangent to both cone walls and the plane.
Mark and label the tangency points on the plane as F1 (#FFFF00) and F2 (#0000FF).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Ice Cream Cone Lemma
lecture_lines: Tangents from a point to a sphere are equal.
This is known as the "Ice Cream Cone Lemma."
Distances from the vertex to the contact circle match.
animations: Draw a white circle (#FFFFFF) representing a sphere and a red point P (#FF0000) outside it.
Draw two tangent segments from P to the circle's boundary.
Flash the two segments and add small white equality marks (#FFFFFF) to show they have equal length.

storyboard.title: The Visual Proof: Linking Segments
lecture_lines: Pick any point $P$ on the elliptical slice.
Connect $P$ to the foci $F_1$ and $F_2$.
$PF_1$ equals the distance to the upper contact circle.
$PF_2$ equals the distance to the lower contact circle.
These segments align along the cone's slant height.
animations: Display the cone, plane, and spheres with a red point P (#FF0000) on the ellipse.
Draw a blue segment (#0000FF) connecting point P to focus F1.
Draw a blue segment from P along the cone's slant to the upper contact circle, labeled A.
Draw an orange-red segment (#FF4500) connecting point P to focus F2.
Draw an orange-red segment from P along the cone's slant to the lower contact circle, labeled B.

storyboard.title: The Constant Sum
lecture_lines: The sum $PF_1 + PF_2$ equals the total slant distance.
This distance $AB$ connects the two fixed circles.
The length $AB$ remains constant as point $P$ moves.
Thus, the sum of distances to foci is constant.
The Dandelin spheres prove this curve is an ellipse.
animations: Highlight segments PF1 and PA in blue (#0000FF) and PF2 and PB in orange-red (#FF4500).
Animate PF1 rotating onto PA and PF2 rotating onto PB to show equality.
Highlight the combined slant segment AB (#00FF00) connecting the two spheres' contact circles.
Display the sum PF1 + PF2 = AB in white text (#FFFFFF) at the top.
Slide point P along the ellipse while the total length AB remains constant.

storyboard.title: Universal Application: Parabolas and Hyperbolas
lecture_lines: Tilting the plane further changes the intersection's shape.
Spheres still reveal the logic of parabolas and hyperbolas.
Geometry and symmetry unite all conic sections.
animations: Show the initial ellipse and green cutting plane (#00FF00).
Tilt the plane until it is parallel to the cone's slant, changing the curve to an orange parabola (#FFA500).
Tilt the plane further to intersect a double cone, forming two pink hyperbola branches (#FFC0CB).
